children.name: Acrocephalus
children.description: Reed warblers — quintessential summer birds of reedbeds and marshy scrub across the Old World, combining remarkable vocal complexity with cryptic brown plumage and elusive habits that make them far more often heard than seen. The family name derives from Greek for 'pointed head', reflecting the flattened crown that gives these birds a characteristic profile as they slip through reed stems. The genus spans from Eurasian breeding species that winter in Africa to island endemics of the Pacific, Mascarene islands, and Indian Ocean.

children.name: Acrocephalus scirpaceus
children.description: The common reed warbler or Eurasian reed-warbler is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus. It breeds across Europe into the temperate western Palaearctic where it is migratory, wintering in sub-Saharan Africa. It is also a resident species over large parts of Africa.

children.name: Acrocephalus arundinaceus
children.description: The great reed warbler is an insectivorous bird in the family Acrocephalidae. It is a medium-sized passerine bird and the largest of the warblers. It breeds throughout mainland Europe and the Western Palearctic and migrates to sub-Saharan Africa in the winter.

children.name: Acrocephalus palustris
children.description: The marsh warbler is an Old World warbler currently classified in the family Acrocephalidae. It breeds in temperate Europe and the western Palearctic and winters mainly in southeast Africa. It is notable for incorporating striking imitations of a wide variety of other birds into its song.

children.name: Acrocephalus melanopogon
children.description: The moustached warbler (Acrocephalus melanopogon) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus schoenobaenus
children.description: The sedge warbler is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus. It is a medium-sized warbler with a brown, streaked back and wings and a distinct pale supercilium. Sedge warblers are migratory, crossing the Sahara to get from their European and Asian breeding grounds to spend winter in Africa.

children.name: Acrocephalus sorghophilus
children.description:
The speckled reed warbler or streaked reed warbler (Acrocephalus sorghophilus) is an Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. The species was first described by Robert Swinhoe in 1863.
It is found in China and the Philippines. Its natural habitats are swamps and arable land. It is threatened by habitat loss, particularly wetland loss in its wintering area of Candaba Swamp.

children.name: Acrocephalus bistrigiceps
children.description:
The black-browed reed warbler (Acrocephalus bistrigiceps) is a marsh-warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It was formerly included in the "Old World warbler" assemblage. The species was first described by Robert Swinhoe in 1860.
It breeds from eastern Mongolia and south-eastern Russia to eastern China and Japan, and winters in Southeast Asia.

children.name: Acrocephalus tangorum
children.description: The Manchurian reed warbler (Acrocephalus tangorum), also known as the Manchurian reed-warbler, is a species of marsh-warbler (family Acrocephalidae). It was formerly included in the "Old World warbler" assemblage, and was usually (and sometimes is still) treated as a subspecies of the paddyfield warbler (A. Agricola). It is found in Cambodia, China, Hong Kong, South Korea, Laos, Russia, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia and possibly Myanmar. Its natural habitat is swamps. It is threatened by habitat loss.

children.name: Acrocephalus dumetorum
children.description: Blyth's reed warbler is a species of reed warbler belonging to the family Acrocephalidae, which also includes the tree warblers. Blyth's reed warbler breeds across the Palearctic zoogeographical region and winters in South Asia. The species has been expanding its range westwards in Europe.

children.name: Acrocephalus concinens
children.description:
The blunt-winged warbler (Acrocephalus concinens) is a marsh-warbler (family Acrocephalidae). The species was first described by Robert Swinhoe in 1870. It was formerly included in the "Old World warbler" assemblage.
It is found in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Northeast India and China; it winters in Myanmar, Thailand and Bangladesh.

children.name: Acrocephalus orientalis
children.description: The Oriental reed warbler (Acrocephalus orientalis) is a passerine bird of eastern Asia belonging to the reed warbler genus Acrocephalus. It was formerly classified as a subspecies of the great reed warbler (A. Arundinaceus) of the western Palearctic.

children.name: Acrocephalus stentoreus
children.description: The clamorous reed warbler (Acrocephalus stentoreus) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus gracilirostris
children.description: The lesser swamp warbler or Cape reed warbler (Acrocephalus gracilirostris) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus. It is sparsely present across sub-Saharan Africa, a common species of reedbeds in standing water.

children.name: Acrocephalus baeticatus
children.description: The common reed warbler or Eurasian reed-warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus rufescens
children.description: The greater swamp warbler (Acrocephalus rufescens) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found in the African countries of Angola, Botswana, Burundi, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Republic of the Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Ghana, Kenya, Mali, Mauritania, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, South Sudan, Tanzania, Togo, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Its natural habitat is swamps.

children.name: Acrocephalus agricola
children.description: The paddyfield warbler is a species of marsh warbler. It was formerly included in the "Old World warbler" assemblage. The Manchurian reed warbler was included in A.

children.name: Acrocephalus paludicola
children.description: ]] The aquatic warbler (Acrocephalus paludicola) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus scirpaceus fuscus
children.description: Sometimes treated as a full species, this eastern form of the Eurasian reed warbler breeds around the Caspian Sea and in Central Asia east to Afghanistan, and is slightly smaller and greyer than the nominate western population. Recent genetic work supports treating it as a separate species, Acrocephalus fuscus, though this treatment remains contested. It winters in East Africa and differs subtly in vocalisation and morphology from western scirpaceus.

children.name: Acrocephalus australis
children.description: The Australian reed warbler (Acrocephalus australis) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus and is the only Acrocephalus species native to Australia. It has also been observed in Papua New Guinea and nearby islands. The name Acrocephalus refers to the peaked crown found on reed warblers in this genus and can be translated to mean "topmost head" in Greek. The species name australis is translated to mean "southern" in Latin, and refers to the species range, Australia. In its western range the Australian reed warbler is also known as "Koordjikotji" (pronounced core'chee'caw'chee) in the local Aboriginal language of Perth and its surrounds.

children.name: Acrocephalus vaughani
children.description:
The Pitcairn reed warbler (Acrocephalus vaughani) is a songbird in the genus Acrocephalus. Formerly placed in the "Old World warbler" assemblage (Sylviidae), it is now in the newly recognized marsh-warbler family Acrocephalidae.
It is endemic to Pitcairn Island in the southern Pacific. Locally known as the "sparrow" (true sparrows are not found on Pitcairn), it used to be common throughout the island, where it is the only land bird.

children.name: Acrocephalus aequinoctialis
children.description:
The bokikokiko, Kiritimati reed warbler or Christmas Island warbler (Acrocephalus aequinoctialis) is a species of warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found only on Kiritimati and Washington Island (Kiribati).
The population size of the bokikokiko is estimated to be around 2500, with a decreasing population trend. The species is under threat from introduced species such as the pig and rat but especially the feral cat and climate change in relation to rising sea levels. This species, along with the Henderson petrel, is currently listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List.

children.name: Acrocephalus caffer
children.description: The Tahiti reed warbler (Acrocephalus caffer) is a songbird in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus familiaris
children.description: The millerbird (Acrocephalus familiaris) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae endemic to the Hawaiian Islands.

children.name: Acrocephalus rehsei
children.description:
The Nauru reed warbler (Acrocephalus rehsei) is a passerine bird endemic to the island of Nauru in the Pacific Ocean. It is one of only two native breeding land-birds on Nauru and it is the only passerine found on the island. It is related to other Micronesian reed warblers, all of which evolved from one of several radiations of the genus across the Pacific. Related warblers on nearby islands include the Caroline reed warbler, with which the Nauru species was initially confused, and the nightingale reed warbler, which was formerly sometimes considered the same species.
A medium-sized warbler, the Nauru reed warbler has dark brown upperparts, cream underparts and a long, thin beak. It makes a low, cup-shaped nest into which it lays two or three white eggs, and it feeds on insects. However, details about its behavior and ecology are little known. It is found throughout Nauru, which has changed substantially in recent decades due to phosphate mining. The Nauru reed warbler is potentially threatened by introduced predators and habitat loss, and its small range means that it could be vulnerable to chance occurrences, such as tropical cyclones. Reports of a similar warbler from nearby islands suggest that it might previously have been found elsewhere, but was driven to local extinction by introduced cats.

children.name: Acrocephalus luscinius
children.description: The nightingale reed warbler (Acrocephalus luscinius), or Guam reed-warbler, is an extinct songbird that was endemic to Guam.

children.name: Acrocephalus syrinx
children.description: The Caroline reed warbler or Caroline Islands reed warbler (Acrocephalus syrinx) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found only on the Caroline Islands in Micronesia.

children.name: Acrocephalus mendanae
children.description:
The southern Marquesan reed warbler (Acrocephalus mendanae) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae.
It was formerly considered conspecific with the northern Marquesan reed warbler, and together known as the Marquesan reed warbler.

children.name: Acrocephalus kerearako
children.description: The Cook reed warbler (Acrocephalus kerearako) or Cook Islands reed warbler, is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is native to the southeastern Cook Islands. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry forests, swamps, and rural gardens. It is threatened by habitat loss.

children.name: Acrocephalus taiti
children.description: The Henderson reed warbler (Acrocephalus taiti), also known as the Henderson reed-warbler or the Henderson Island reed warbler, is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found only on Henderson Island, part of the Pitcairn Islands. Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical dry forests. It is threatened by habitat loss.

children.name: Acrocephalus rimatarae
children.description: The Rimatara reed warbler (Acrocephalus rimitarae) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found only in Rimatara in French Polynesia. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry forests and swamps. Due to its limited geographic distribution, this bird is classified as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species.

children.name: Acrocephalus luscinia
children.description: The nightingale reed warbler (Acrocephalus luscinius), or Guam reed-warbler, is an extinct songbird that was endemic to Guam.

children.name: Acrocephalus griseldis
children.description:
The Basra reed warbler (Acrocephalus griseldis) is a "warbler" of the genus Acrocephalus. It is a near-endemic breeder in the Tigris–Euphrates river system in southwestern Iran, eastern and southern Iraq, and Kuwait, though it has also recently colonised wetlands in Israel. It breeds in extensive beds of papyrus and reeds. It is easily mistaken for the great reed warbler but is a bit smaller, has whiter underparts and has a narrower, longer and more pointed bill. It is migratory, wintering in East Africa. It is a very rare vagrant in Europe. The call is a gruff chaar, deeper than that of a common reed warbler.
It is found in aquatic vegetation in or around shallow, fresh or brackish water, still or flowing, mainly in dense reedbeds. It is found in thickets and bushland when migrating or wintering.

children.name: Acrocephalus cinnamomeus
children.description: The common reed warbler or Eurasian reed-warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus newtoni
children.description: The Madagascar swamp warbler (Acrocephalus newtoni) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found only in Madagascar. Its natural habitat is swamps.

children.name: Acrocephalus longirostris
children.description: Moorea reed warbler (Acrocephalus longirostris) is a species of songbird in the genus Acrocephalus. Formerly placed in the "Old World warbler" assemblage (Sylviidae), it is now in the newly recognized marsh warbler family Acrocephalidae. It was once considered a subspecies of the Tahiti reed warbler.

children.name: Acrocephalus immacula
children.description: A small, plain reed warbler endemic to Rodrigues Island in the Mascarenes, now extinct, known only from sub-fossil bones and historical accounts. It likely occupied reed beds and scrub along the island's watercourses before habitat destruction and introduced predators (particularly rats and cats) drove it to extinction, probably in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Its bones were described in conjunction with the many other Rodrigues extinction-era fauna; it may have survived long enough to be observed by early settlers but was never formally collected.

children.name: Hippolais
children.description: Hippolais warblers — medium-sized, active warblers of scrub and garden habitats with loud, complex songs that include mimicry of other species. The icterine warbler (härmsångare) is the most familiar member of the genus in Sweden: a yellow-green bird with a distinctively angular, peaked crown that breeds in parks, gardens, and mixed woodland edge throughout the country. Its song is a rich, tumbling medley of musical phrases, harsh notes, and imitated sounds delivered with great energy from prominent perches — one of the most complex and attractive warbler songs in Sweden. The Swedish name härmsångare ('mimic singer') perfectly captures the bird's talent for weaving snatches of other species' songs into its own performance.

children.name: Hippolais icterina
children.description: The icterine warbler is an Old World warbler in the tree warbler genus Hippolais. It breeds in mainland Europe except the southwest, where it is replaced by its western counterpart, the melodious warbler. It is migratory, wintering in sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Hippolais polyglotta
children.description: The melodious warbler (Hippolais polyglotta) is an Old World warbler in the tree warbler genus Hippolais.

children.name: Hippolais olivetorum
children.description: The olive-tree warbler (Hippolais olivetorum) is a species of passerine bird in the family Acrocephalidae, the reed and tree warblers. It breeds in southeast Europe and the Near East. It is migratory, wintering in eastern and southern Africa, from Kenya south to South Africa.

children.name: Hippolais pallida
children.description: The eastern olivaceous warbler (Iduna pallida), known simply as the olivaceous warbler when its western relative is referred to as the 'isabelline warbler', is a small passerine bird with drab plumage tones, that is native to the Old World.

children.name: Hippolais opaca
children.description: The western olivaceous warbler (Iduna opaca), also known as the isabelline warbler, is a "warbler", formerly placed in the Old World warblers when these were a paraphyletic wastebin taxon.

children.name: Hippolais languida
children.description:
Upcher's warbler (Hippolais languida) is an Old World warbler in the tree warbler genus Hippolais. It breeds in an area from Turkey south and east to Pakistan. It is migratory, wintering in eastern Africa, from Eritrea and Somalia south to Tanzania.
This small passerine bird is a species found in semi-desert habitats, frequenting bushy scrub and thickets of tamarisk. Four or five eggs are laid in a nest in bushes and low trees.

children.name: Iduna
children.description: Iduna warblers — a group of small to medium-sized unstreaked warblers split from Hippolais following phylogenetic work showing they form a separate clade. They span Africa and Asia, typically inhabiting dry scrub, acacia thickets, and semi-arid scrubland, and share a general brownish-grey plumage with subtle differences in supercilium prominence, bill length, and tail-wagging behaviour. Several are part of a species complex whose boundaries remain debated.

children.name: Iduna caligata
children.description: The booted warbler is a species of passerine bird belonging to the family Acrocephalidae, the reed and tree warblers. This species breeds in Eastern Europe and western Asia, wintering in south Asia. it is a regular vagrant to Western Europe.

children.name: Iduna rama
children.description: Sykes's warbler (Iduna rama) is an Old World warbler in the tree warbler family. It was formerly considered a subspecies of the booted warbler, but is now considered a full species. Its breeding range is from northeast Arabia to Turkestan, west China and Afghanistan. Like the booted warbler, many populations of the species migrate in winter to the Indian subcontinent as far south as Sri Lanka.

children.name: Iduna pallida
children.description: The eastern olivaceous warbler (Iduna pallida), known simply as the olivaceous warbler when its western relative is referred to as the 'isabelline warbler', is a small passerine bird with drab plumage tones, that is native to the Old World.

children.name: Iduna opaca
children.description: The western olivaceous warbler (Iduna opaca), also known as the isabelline warbler, is a "warbler", formerly placed in the Old World warblers when these were a paraphyletic wastebin taxon.

children.name: Iduna nana
children.description: The smallest member of the genus, a delicate, pale warbler of semi-arid scrub, tamarisk and low thorn-bush from Kazakhstan and Central Asia south to northwestern India. Its specific epithet nana refers to its diminutive size. It is an active, tail-flicking species that sings a faint, rapid song from within dense low cover; its song is easily overlooked. The species winters in the Indian subcontinent and is very rarely recorded outside its core Central Asian and South Asian range.

children.name: Iduna languida
children.description: A large Iduna of freshwater marshes, reed beds and riverside vegetation in the Middle East, breeding in the marshes of Iraq and Iran and wintering in East Africa. It is one of the least-known members of the family, with limited data on its population size, though it was historically common in the extensive Mesopotamian marshes. The draining of the Iraqi marshes in the 1990s devastated its core breeding habitat, though partial restoration since 2003 has allowed some recovery. Larger and heavier than most congeners.

children.name: Chloropeta
children.description: African yellow warblers — a small genus of brightly coloured warblers endemic to sub-Saharan Africa, occupying tall grass, papyrus, reed beds, and forest edges near water. Their yellow underparts and greenish-olive upperparts make them among the most distinctively coloured members of the family, contrasting sharply with the drab browns of most Acrocephalus. They are closely associated with tall marsh vegetation and can be remarkably skulking despite their bright plumage.

children.name: Calamonastides
children.description: A monotypic genus containing a single distinctive African reed warbler, related to Acrocephalus but placed in its own genus based on morphological and molecular distinctiveness. It inhabits papyrus swamps and reed beds in East Africa.

children.name: Calamonastides gracilirostris
children.description: The papyrus yellow warbler, papyrus flycatcher-warbler or thin-billed flycatcher-warbler (Calamonastides gracilirostris) is a species of tree warbler; formerly, these were placed in the paraphyletic "Old World warblers". It is monotypic in its genus. It is found in Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia. Its natural habitat is swamps. It is threatened by habitat loss.

children.name: Calamocichla
children.description: African swamp warblers — a genus of large, heavily built reed warblers from sub-Saharan Africa, formerly placed within Acrocephalus. They occupy papyrus swamps, reed beds and tall riverine vegetation and are among the most robust members of the family. Their loud, churring songs are prominent in African wetland soundscapes.

children.name: Calamocichla rufescens
children.description: A large, dark brown swamp warbler specialising in papyrus and tall reed beds across central and East Africa, from Senegal east to Kenya and south to Angola. It is a prominent papyrus-zone bird whose loud, churring song is one of the defining sounds of lowland African swamps. Notably sedentary, it is reluctant to cross open water between swamp fragments, leading to population isolation across the papyrus archipelago of the Congo basin and Albertine Rift.

children.name: Calamocichla gracilirostris
children.description: Africa's most widespread and common swamp warbler, occupying papyrus, Phragmites reed beds, and tall sedge beds from Ethiopia south to South Africa. It shows considerable subspecific variation across its extensive range and has a rich, bubbling song that is a familiar wetland sound across the continent. An important Cuculus cuckoo host in many parts of Africa, with cuckoo egg mimicry having co-evolved with local warbler egg colouration in some populations.

children.name: Calamocichla lopezi
children.description: A montane swamp warbler restricted to highland marshes and bog edges in the Cameroon highlands and Bioko Island in the Gulf of Guinea, at elevations above 1,500 m. It inhabits rank grass, bracken, and sedge at bog margins rather than lowland papyrus, reflecting a distinct altitudinal niche from its congeners. Poorly known and seldom observed, it was long treated as a race of the greater swamp warbler but differs in size, structure and song from lowland relatives.

children.name: Nesillas
children.description: Malagasy brush warblers — a genus of five secretive, long-tailed warblers endemic to Madagascar and the Comoro Islands, occupying dense undergrowth in humid forest, coastal scrub, and degraded vegetation. They are among the most elusive passerines in Madagascar, far more often heard than seen, creeping through dense vegetation like diminutive bush-warblers. Their taxonomy has been revised several times and their relationships within Acrocephalidae are still being clarified.

children.name: Nesillas typica
children.description: The Malagasy brush warbler (Nesillas typica), also known as the Madagascar brush warbler, is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae.. The Malagasy brush warbler is a widespread species of forest undergrowth and is found primarily in both Madagascar and the Comoro Islands. The bird is typically found alone or in pairs of 2 and flies short distances due to a small wingspan. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry forests, subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests, and subtropical or tropical moist shrubland.

children.name: Nesillas lantzii
children.description: The subdesert brush warbler (Nesillas lantzii), also known as Lantz's brush-warbler, is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found only in Madagascar.

children.name: Nesillas mariae
children.description: The Moheli brush warbler (Nesillas mariae) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found only in Comoros. Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical moist montane forests.

children.name: Nesillas brevicaudata
children.description: The Grande Comore brush warbler (Nesillas brevicaudata) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae. It is found in Comoros and Mayotte. Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical moist montane forests.

children.name: Nesillas aldabranus
children.description: Declared extinct in the 1980s, the Aldabra brush warbler was known from a tiny area of dense coastal scrub on Aldabra Atoll, Seychelles. It was last recorded in 1983, and despite the protected status of Aldabra — a UNESCO World Heritage Site — the species could not be saved, likely succumbing to introduced cats and black rats. It is one of the few twentieth-century extinctions of a bird on a currently well-protected island, highlighting how quickly small populations can collapse even in reserves.

children.name: Bebrornis
children.description: Indian Ocean island warblers — a small genus of reed warblers from the Seychelles and Rodrigues, sometimes merged into Acrocephalus. Both species are highly threatened island endemics that have been subjects of intensive conservation intervention, with the Seychelles warbler becoming a celebrated case study in island bird recovery.

children.name: Bebrornis rodericanus
children.description: The Rodrigues warbler (Acrocephalus rodericanus) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae.

children.name: Bebrornis sechellensis
children.description: The Seychelles warbler (Acrocephalus sechellensis), also known as Seychelles brush warbler, is a small songbird found on five granitic and corraline islands in the Seychelles.

children.name: Amphilais
children.description: A monotypic genus containing a single secretive Malagasy warbler of rank grass and scrub, whose affinities within Acrocephalidae were debated until molecular work confirmed its placement. Like Nesillas, it is an elusive ground-level creeper of Madagascar's humid habitats.

children.name: Amphilais seebohmi
children.description: The grey emutail (Bradypterus seebohmi), also known as the Madagascan grassbird or feather-tailed warbler, is an emutail in the family Locustellidae.

children.name: Thamnornis
children.description: A monotypic genus of Madagascar, containing a single species of dry forest and spiny scrub. The genus was long of uncertain family placement but is now confirmed in Acrocephalidae. It occupies the unique xerophytic habitats of southwestern Madagascar.

children.name: Thamnornis chloropetoides
children.description:
The thamnornis or thamnornis warbler (Thamnornis chloropetoides) is a species of Malagasy warbler in the family Bernieridae. It is endemic to Madagascar, where it is restricted to the spiny forest of the island's southwest. It is greyish above and whitish below, with narrow green fringes to the wing feathers and a marked supercilium. The outer tail-feathers have pale tips.
Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry forests and subtropical or tropical dry shrubland. It is usually seen near the ground, but sings from tall trees. It often associates in family groups or with Newtonias in mixed-species flocks. While not considered threatened, its population is inferred to be decreasing due to widespread deforestation across its range.

children.name: Randia
children.description: A monotypic genus of Madagascar, recently described and recognised as a distinct genus within Acrocephalidae. It inhabits dry forests and the ecotone between humid and dry zones in Madagascar.

children.name: Randia pseudozosterops
children.description:
Rand's warbler (Randia pseudozosterops) is a species in the family Bernieridae. It is found only in Madagascar, where it is restricted to the island's eastern rainforests. It is grey above and unmarked pale below, with a strong pale supercilium. The bill is strong and slightly decurved, with some individuals possessing a pale orange lower mandible.
Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests, where it is fairly common up to 1200 m. It frequently joins mixed-species flocks, where it often feeds along horizontal or angled branches. It also tends to sing for long periods from the canopy. While not considered threatened, its population is inferred to be decreasing due to widespread deforestation across its range.
